caseno: Memorandum of Appeal from Original Decree No. 495 of 1991.
lawyer:
Shantiranjan Karmaker  with Md. Abdus Salam Mondal, Advocates -----For the Appellant 
No one ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Pratik Bandhu Roy and others ----- Appellants
Vs
Alok Bandhu Roy and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Choudhury J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 27-8-94 passed by the learned District Judge, Rajshahi in Miscellaneous Case No. 29 of 1983. The learned District Judge by the said order rejected the appellant's prayer for probate of a Will. 

 2. The short fact leading to this appeal is that, one Sree Anil Bandhu Roy, son of late Akhil Bandhu Roy was the owner of certain lands and before his death on 22-4-1979 he executed his last will on 15-4-79 which was executed in presence of some witnesses. By that will he bequeathed his properties situated within the District of Rajshahi in favour of the present appellant. Thereafter on 23-2-1983 the present appellant instituted Miscellaneous case No. 29 of 1983 before the learned District Judge, Rajshahi and prayed for granting him letters of administration. The case was accordingly registered and notices have been duly issued and served. Thereafter, after examination of 3 witnesses the District Judge by his order dated 27 -8-84 dismissed the miscellaneous case ex parte. The appellant then being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid order preferred this appeal. 

 6. These are the witnesses examined before the trial Court to prove the execution of Ext. 1 by the testator. The learned Advocate for the appellant contends that there are three direct witnesses who deposed on the execution of Ext. 1 by the testator. Placing reliance in the case of Ryali Kameswara Raovs. Bendapudi Suryaprakasarao & ors, reported in AIR 1962 (Andra) 178, the learned Advocate contends that even if there is slight difference in the signatures that cannot by itself be a ground to disbelieve the document in view of the evidence of three direct witnesses who were present at the time of execution of the will by the testator. In the said decision it has been held that the fact that the signature was in shaky handwriting did not raise suspicion as to its genuineness as three direct witnesses proved the signatures of the testator. The learned Advocate further contends that though notices have been served on the Deputy Commissioner and there was a public notification of the presentation of the case before the learned District Judge but none came forward with any objection as to the issuance of the letter of administration. The trial Court merely compared the signatures and disbelieved Ext.1. But it has been held in the case of Kessarbai vs. Tethabai Jivan, reported in AIR 1928 (PC) 277 that mere comparison of admitted signatures without expert advice or microscopic examination is dangerous and according to Mr. Karmaker it is hazardous. It has also been held in the case of Surendra Mohan Basu vs. Saroj Ranjan Sarkar, reported in AIR 1961 (Cal) 491 that while it is competent on the part of Judge or a Magistrate to compare the disputed signature with the admitted signatures for himself, it is unsafe to rely entirely on such personal comparison. Here in the present case none has disputed the signature and nobody came forward to depose that the signatures of the testator is forged and fabricated. Mr. Karmaker submits that it is only the trial Court that found fault with these signatures without comparing the same with any other admitted signatures. 

 7. We have carefully gone through the signatures and it appears that the trial Court though found that the signatures on page 2 are different as the executants firstly wrote “শ্রী অনিল বন্ধু রায়” and then wrote “শ্রী অনিল বন্ধু রায়” But from a close scrutiny it appears that the executants also wrote Ashi Bandhu Roy first and when the writing was somewhat defective he corrected it by writing his name again just below the final one and there is no difference between these two writings. It is admitted that the testator was ill when he executed the document and he died immediately thereafter. From the papers filed it appears that the will was executed on 15-5-1979 and the testator died on 22-5-1979 and in such a situation it is natural to sign like this and that has been done in the present case. Furthermore, three witnesses have been examined which included the present appellant but the trial Court, it appears, without discarding the evidence of these witnesses and merely comparing the signatures by naked eyes came to the finding that the will cannot be probated. This is a sweeping order passed by the trial Court. Before passing any such order the trial Court ought to have discussed the evidence. We have considered the evidence and it appears that three witnesses deposed on oath that in their presence Sree Anil Bandhu Roy executed the will and there is nothing before us to disbelieve them. We have also carefully looked into the will Ext. 1 and also gone through the evidence of three witnesses and we hold that the appellant has succeeded in proving the case and he is entitled to a probate of the will. 

 9. Thus, after consideration of the materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocate for the appellant, we hold that the learned District Judge has committed wrong and illegality in passing the impugned order which requires interference. This is a fit case where this Court should interfere and set aside the judgment and order passed by the District Judge, Rajshahi in Miscellaneous Case No. 29 of 1983. 

 10. The appeal is accordingly, allowed. The Judgment and order dated 27-8-1984 passed by the District Judge is hereby set aside and the miscellaneous case, that is, Miscellaneous Case No. 29 of 1983 is hereby allowed. The will is accordingly, probated.
